_README: Started by init.py from Ms Pac-Man (NTSC) (Atari) (1987) (E42FC700).a78.
Every human judgement about this ROM lives in this file; the
generated listings are disposable, so renaming is free.
What to do next, roughly in order:
Read the coverage it reports. Low coverage is normal at
first and is the number you are trying to move.
2. Every unresolved indirect jump it reports is a hole. Add the
target to `entries`, or the pointer pair to `ram_vectors` if
the handler is installed into RAM.
Finds the sound code and the tables feeding it.
4. Name things in `labels` as soon as you know what they are.
See docs/method.md for the working order and docs/pitfalls.md for
the traps that each cost real time.

comments.rom:F61A: CONFIRMED LIVE, first live-verified finding for this project. The score-add routine: zeroes ram_00B9/ram_00BA, then BCD-adds a 4-byte value (ram_00B9-ram_00BC) into the current player's score -- Score (ram_0046-0049, 4 bytes/8 BCD digits) if ram_0042==0 and ram_0045==0, else Score2 (ram_004C-004F) for the other branch. Since ram_00B9/00BA are always zeroed by this routine itself before the add, only ScoreDeltaHi (ram_00BB) and ScoreDeltaLo (ram_00BC) ever carry a real value -- i.e. every caller stages the actual point award into just these two bytes (up to BCD 9999) before calling here. Found by grepping for SED (4 sites total in this ROM, the same short-candidate-list technique used throughout the sibling projects) rather than guessing.
comments.rom:E026: CONFIRMED LIVE and screenshot-verified -- this is the user's 'Teddy Bear gave 50 points as a fruit' hint, directly resolved. dat_E0EB (high BCD digit pair) and dat_E0F3 (low BCD digit pair), both indexed by CurrentFruitType (ram_2116), are the fruit point-value table -- and at a x10-per-unit BCD scale (the same scaling convention independently found in the Galaga project's own score accumulator), they match the manual's fruit table EXACTLY across all 8 entries: Teddy Bear 50, Cherries 100, Strawberry 200, Orange 500, Pretzel 700, Apple 1,000, Pear 2,000, Banana 5,000 (the last three needing the high-byte table's $01/$02/$05 to reach four digits, since the low byte alone caps at BCD 99). LIVE-VERIFIED against run-02.inp: at frame 3,011, ScoreDeltaHi/Lo are set to $00/$05 (CurrentFruitType=0, i.e. Teddy Bear) right as ScoreDigit/on-screen score jumps from 2160 to 2210 -- and a screenshot at that exact frame shows Ms. Pac-Man directly overlapping a distinct brown, round, non-ghost sprite (no eyes, unlike all four ghosts) at the ghost-house exit, consistent with the fruit item. A second event at frame 7,372 (CurrentFruitType=1, Cherries) awards exactly +100, matching the table's second entry. What still isn't confirmed: what actually sets CurrentFruitType (i.e. what decides which fruit appears when), and whether it's capped at 7 (Banana) or can go higher -- directly relevant to the user's third hint about the level-name sequence appearing to plateau at Banana rather than moving to 'random fruit' as the manual describes.
comments.rom:E084: The ghost-eating chain point-value table, structurally analogous to the fruit table at rom:E026 -- dat_E0E3 (high BCD digit pair: $00,$00,$00,$01) / dat_E0E7 (low BCD digit pair: $20,$40,$80,$60), indexed by GhostChainCount (ram_00FE, incremented once per ghost eaten within a single power-pellet frightened window). At the same x10-per-unit BCD scale as the fruit table, the four paired entries read as 200/400/800/1,600 -- the classic arcade Pac-Man ghost-chain progression exactly. LIVE-CONFIRMED for the first three (frames 2239/2492/2613 in run-02.inp, matching a '200' score-popup screenshotted directly during this investigation); the fourth (1,600) is read from the table only -- no 4th-consecutive-ghost event appeared in the recording checked so far.
comments.rom:D508: SOLVES the user's third hint directly ('the levels change to a point and banana appears to be the last fruit since I beat that level and it stayed banana') -- and it is NOT the manual-vs-ROM divergence this project first guessed it might be. This is where CurrentFruitType (ram_2116, see rom:E026) gets chosen for a new level: if WaveCounter (ram_00A6, newly named) is less than 8, CurrentFruitType is set directly to WaveCounter -- a clean sequential march through the 8 named fruits, matching the manual's own Teddy Bear-through-Banana progression exactly. Once WaveCounter reaches 8 or higher, the manual's own claim ('random fruit mazes') kicks in structurally: a PRNG call (rom:sub_F505) masked to 0-7 picks a fruit -- BUT the result must satisfy `result >= FruitTypeFloor` (ram_0040, newly named) via a rejection-sampling retry loop, or it's discarded and re-rolled. FruitTypeFloor is the SAME byte the title screen's 'USE JOYSTICK TO CHANGE SETTINGS' level-select cursor writes to (rom:sub_E85B increments it up to a clamp of 7, rom:sub_E86A decrements it down to a floor of 0) -- i.e. whatever starting level the player picks on the title screen becomes a PERMANENT lower bound on every 'random' fruit draw for the rest of that game. Starting from Banana (FruitTypeFloor=7) leaves exactly one value (7) that can ever pass the retry check -- every wave-9-plus draw is Banana, forced, not by chance. LIVE-CONFIRMED across all four of this project's recordings, cleanly cross-validated: run-01 (started at Banana, FruitTypeFloor=7) shows CurrentFruitType locked at 7 for the entire rest of the recording (tens of thousands of frames, many waves); run-03 (started at Pear, FruitTypeFloor=6) shows CurrentFruitType oscillating only between 6 and 7, the exact two values that satisfy >=6; run-04 (started at Pretzel, FruitTypeFloor=5) oscillates among 5/6/7; run-02 (started at Teddy Bear, FruitTypeFloor=0) shows genuinely varied values (0,1,2,3,4,6 all seen), the unconstrained case matching the manual's plain description. The manual's 'random fruit' claim is true in general -- this project's own earlier flagged 'discrepancy' was really just one specific playthrough's starting choice producing a degenerate, single-outcome case of a genuinely-random mechanism, not a bug or a port divergence.
comments.rom:CD21: Directly relevant to the user's second hint (intermissions appear after the Strawberry and Apple level wins) and their follow-up suggestion that chasing it would help classify data blocks -- both panned out. WaveCounter (ram_00A6) advances here on every level clear; alongside it, MazeScheduleIndex (ram_00A7, newly named) advances too, wrapping from 14 back down to 6 rather than to 0 -- so after the initial 0-13 run-up, it cycles through 6-13 forever. MazeScheduleIndex indexes dat_D03A (14 bytes: $FF,$FF,$00,$FF,$FF,$01,$FF,$FF,$FF,$02,$FF,$FF,$FF,$02) -- $FF (negative, caught by a BMI check) means 'keep the current maze', any other value is a real maze index (0-2 seen) passed to rom:sub_E0FB to actually reload it. Reading the non-$FF positions directly: maze changes happen exactly at wave-index 2 and 5 -- Strawberry and Apple, matching the user's hint precisely -- plus two more at 9 and 13 (both loading maze 2) that the user didn't mention, likely because by wave 9+ CurrentFruitType has already left the named sequence (see rom:D508) and these transitions may be less visually distinct or not accompanied by an intermission at all. After wave 13, the repeating 6-13 cycle keeps landing on maze 2 (indices 9 and 13 both point there, everything else in the cycle is $FF/keep-current) -- the maze effectively stops changing once the player is far enough in, the same 'permanently locked' shape found in the Banana fruit mechanism (see rom:D508) but for maze layout instead of fruit type. RESOLVED -- see rom:E0FB: the intermission animation IS in there, a blocking wait-loop after three special actor sprites are set up, easy to walk past at first read because the surrounding code also handles the mundane 'clear old sprites, load the new maze index' housekeeping in the same routine.
comments.rom:CD56: A companion table to the maze-change schedule at rom:CD21, also indexed by MazeScheduleIndex (ram_00A7): dat_D02C (14 bytes: $00,$00,$00,$01,$01,$01,$02,$02,$02,$02,$03,$03,$03,$03) feeds MazeColorVariant (ram_00A5, newly named). Unlike dat_D03A (mostly 'keep current maze'), this one cycles cleanly through all 4 values -- a plausible candidate for a maze color/palette variant selector (matching the manual's 'four different maze patterns' more directly than dat_D03A's own 0-2 range), but not yet confirmed live against what MazeColorVariant actually controls on screen.
comments.rom:CD5E: CONFIRMED: dat_CF51 (one of the day-one 'mixed-signature' blocks this project couldn't classify further at the time) is genuine graphics/display-list data, not a jump or parameter table -- this routine copies it directly into $1F00+ (alongside dat_CFAA and dat_CFB1, both sub-offsets within the same declared dat_CF51 block), the working display area Maria renders from. Called from three sites (rom:CBDB, rom:CC6A, rom:E658), consistent with a general maze/HUD graphics (re)load rather than something tied to one specific maze variant, since the same source data is copied every time regardless of which maze is active. First concrete resolution of one of the nineteen originally-unclassified small data blocks from day one.
comments.rom:E0FB: SOLVES the user's second hint directly ('a couple of intermission animations, the strawberry and apple level wins appear to be where those are located') -- the actual cutscene code, not just the maze-change schedule that correlates with it (see rom:CD21). This routine is only called when a MazeScheduleIndex (ram_00A7) entry in dat_D03A is a real maze index rather than $FF -- i.e. exactly at wave-index 2, 5, 9, and 13. What it actually does: stores the new maze index into ram_2124, clears/hides four normal sprite slots (rom:CD83), sets up THREE special actor sprites via rom:sub_E168 (reading dat_E348/dat_E34B/dat_E354/dat_E35D for slots X=0,1,2 -- matching what a screenshot at this exact live event showed: a Pac-Man-like character, a Ms. Pac-Man-like character, and a ghost, moving across an otherwise-black screen with no maze walls, the classic Ms. Pac-Man 'hallway' intermission), then BLOCKS in a wait loop -- `L_E150: JSR sub_CB25; LDA ram_1D00; BNE L_E150` -- calling the general per-frame update repeatedly until ram_1D00 (slot 0's 'still active' flag in the same per-actor array rom:sub_EA36 also reads, ram_1D00,X) reaches zero, i.e. until the cutscene's own actor naturally finishes and clears itself. Only after that does sub_E0FB return and the normal 'load the next maze' sequence (rom:sub_CD56, rom:sub_CC1F, etc., already mapped) proceed. LIVE-VERIFIED against run-02.inp: screenshotted the actual animation (frames 13,400-13,540, wave-index 2->3, i.e. the Strawberry level win) and confirmed ram_1D00 reads 1 throughout that exact window, dropping to 0 at frame 13,510 -- right before the new maze begins rendering in the next screenshot. The other two milestone waves (9 and 13, both loading maze 2) go through the identical code path and should trigger the same animation, though the user didn't report seeing those specifically -- plausibly because by wave 9+ the named fruit sequence has already ended (see rom:D508) and those transitions may be less memorable, not because the mechanism differs.
comments.rom:CC01: Directly resolves the user's first hint's other half: 'the teddy bear level runs slowly'. FruitTypeFloor (ram_0040, the title-screen level-select cursor) is copied straight into WaveCounter here (and again at rom:CC13 a few instructions later, for the second player). So picking a starting level on the title screen doesn't just choose a fruit icon and a maze -- it seeds the real difficulty/wave progression counter directly. Choosing Teddy Bear starts the game at WaveCounter=0, the very first wave of the game's normal per-wave speed curve, not a separate 'slow practice mode'. See rom:DAA7 for how WaveCounter turns into an actual on-screen speed.
comments.rom:DAA7: The per-wave speed lookup. WaveCounter is clamped to a max index of $13 (19) and used to index dat_DCF9 (20 bytes), landing in WaveSpeedPeriod (ram_00F3, newly named). dat_DCF9[0] (wave 0, i.e. Teddy Bear start) is $C0 (192) -- by far the largest value in the whole table (next is $B4/180 at wave 1, then it falls into the $1E-$96/30-150 range from wave 4 on). WaveSpeedPeriod is copied into SpeedCountdown (ram_00DC) whenever Pac-Man's actor is (re)spawned each wave (rom:sub_DAC3/rom:sub_DAF8, both via rom:sub_EA36). See rom:DC44 for how a bigger period value becomes visibly slower movement, and rom:CC01 for how the title-screen level-select choice seeds WaveCounter (and so this lookup) directly.
comments.rom:DC44: The live movement-cadence gate that WaveSpeedPeriod (ram_00F3, see rom:DAA7) ultimately controls. Runs every frame but only acts on alternating frames (ram_00A1 AND #$01), decrementing SpeedCountdown (ram_00DC) and firing a movement step (rom:sub_DC0F or rom:sub_DC1A) only when the counter's value (before the decrement) matches one of five fixed checkpoints in dat_DC6B or dat_DC70 -- a fractional-speed cadence scheme with a fixed number of 'step' checkpoints spread across a counter that resets to WaveSpeedPeriod. A bigger period spreads those same five checkpoints across more real frames, so movement steps land far less often per unit of time -- visibly slower motion. CONFIRMED LIVE in run-02.inp (the Teddy Bear-start recording): at frame 2144, right as real (non-attract-demo) play begins, SpeedCountdown loads to 192 and visibly counts down 1 per 2 frames (the alternating-frame gate); later in the same recording, wave 4 loads a period of 90 and wave 5 loads 60, each noticeably faster. Wave 0/Teddy Bear's 192 is the slowest period in the entire dat_DCF9 table, confirming the user's 'runs slowly' hint is just the ordinary, slowest tier of the game's built-in per-wave difficulty curve, not a distinct mode.
comments.rom:FC18: The real maze wall-layout loader. Indexes a 4-entry pointer table by MazeColorVariant (dat_FC84 for the low byte, dat_FC88's first 4 bytes for the high byte -- both auto-labeled sub-offsets inside the dat_FC7C tail block) to get one of $FCC8/$FD7C/$FE30/$FEE4, then copies 128 bytes from there into MazeBitmapBuffer (ram_1C00, newly named). That buffer is a compact bitwise encoding of the maze's walls -- rom:sub_FC00/L_FB53 reads it 1 byte at a time and unpacks each byte's 8 bits via 8 calls to rom:sub_FBAA, which (through dat_FBBC/dat_FBDC, see their own note) picks the correct wall-corner/edge tile code for each bit position and pokes it into the screen's tile buffer. This is the actual maze-layout data the user expected most of the ROM to be -- just autotile-encoded rather than stored as a literal per-cell grid, which is why the two blocks originally guessed as 'maze data' (dat_E342, dat_EB75) turned out to be something else entirely (see their own notes).
comments.rom:D713: The per-ghost-slot movement dispatcher, called once per ghost per movement step. Branches on GhostState (ram_2138,X): nonzero -> a single fixed target near the house door (rom:sub_D73F, $0A,$0F) -- eaten eyes heading home. GhostState==0 then branches on GhostFrightFlag (ram_2140,X): nonzero -> pure random-direction wandering (rom:sub_D72F) -- a frightened ghost. Otherwise branches on ChaseModeFlag (ram_00FF): nonzero -> rom:sub_D74A (the wave-start / timed 'not chasing' mode); zero -> rom:sub_D777, the real targeting AI (see its own comment). LIVE-VERIFIED against run-02.inp via tools/probe-ghostlogic.lua: GhostFrightFlag flips 0->8 for all 4 ghosts simultaneously at frame 2144, hits exactly 16 at frames 2240/2493/2614 (matching the independently-verified ghost-eaten frames from rom:E084's comment), and GhostState runs the predicted 1->3->4->2->0 cycle repeatedly for each eaten ghost.
comments.rom:D777: CONFIRMED: this replicates the arcade's four distinct ghost-targeting personalities almost exactly, keyed off the ghost's own slot number (X): X==2 ('Inky'): rom:L_D7D0 computes 2x the vector from slot 0's own position (ram_2128/ram_212C, i.e. 'Blinky') to a point offset ahead of Pac-Man in his current facing direction (dat_DCF1/dat_DCF5) -- the textbook Inky double-vector algorithm. X==1 ('Pinky'): rom:L_D7B8 targets a fixed offset ahead of Pac-Man in his facing direction (dat_DCE9/dat_DCED) -- the textbook Pinky 'ambush' algorithm. X>=3 ('Sue'/Clyde): rom:L_D7F2 measures actual distance from the ghost's own position to Pac-Man for a distance-gated chase-or-flee decision -- the textbook Clyde/Sue algorithm. X==0 ('Blinky', the fallthrough default): targets Pac-Man's current position directly, with an extra check that sets ram_2144 to a nonzero speed-boost code as dots run low -- a plausible 'Cruise Elroy' implementation, clarified further on a second pass: it's gated on ram_213B (GhostState for slot 3, 'Sue'/Clyde -- the LAST ghost released per the staggered dat_E8AA thresholds) being exactly 0 (out of the house, roaming) before it even checks the dots-remaining thresholds -- i.e. Elroy can't engage until every ghost has left the house, using the last-released slot as a stand-in for checking all four individually. Only once that gate passes does it compare dots-remaining ($F0 - DotsEatenCount) against CruiseElroyThreshold1/2 (themselves keyed by MazeColorVariant, see rom:DE8B). RETRACTED: an earlier pass claimed this was live-confirmed activating in run-02.inp -- wrong, see rom:DEF7's comment for the correction. The speed-boost effect itself still isn't live-verified against an actual movement-speed change, and neither is genuine Elroy activation (as opposed to the misattributed event previously reported).
comments.rom:D74A: The alternate, non-chase movement mode selected by ChaseModeFlag (ram_00FF) != 0 -- entered once at every wave start (rom:sub_DA32) and cleared back to chase mode by a timed, queued transition (see rom:sub_DB35). For X==2/X==3 it targets a fixed corner tile ($1C,$1A / $1C,$01 respectively) -- classic scatter-mode corner behavior. For X==0/X==1 it instead picks a uniformly random direction (rom:L_D751), the same random-walk primitive rom:sub_D72F uses for frightened ghosts -- an asymmetry worth double-checking live (only 2 of the 4 slots get an actual scatter corner here; not yet confirmed whether that's a real simplification in this port or a misreading of which slot is which).
comments.rom:D69B: The per-frame chase/scatter mode-timer tick, called once per frame from the main loop (rom:sub_D679). Only advances the elapsed-time counter pair (ram_00FB/ram_00FC) while SpeedCountdown reads 0 -- in practice this means it free-runs every frame during idle/pre-spawn stretches (e.g. the 'READY' pause) and only occasionally otherwise, once per movement-cadence wrap (see rom:sub_DC44). ram_00FC is the fast, wrapping (0-255) counter; ram_00FB only increments on ram_00FC's wrap. The firing condition is NOT a clean 16-bit magnitude compare -- it's two independent gates ANDed together: ram_00FB >= ModeTimerTargetLo (ram_216C) AND ram_00FC >= ram_216D, checked every tick. Once ram_00FB first crosses its threshold it stays true forever (monotonic), so the effective trigger becomes 'the next time ram_00FC's repeating climb crosses ram_216D' -- confirmed LIVE against run-02.inp via tools/probe-modeschedule2.lua. Once that's true (and ram_216C isn't the $FF sentinel), calls rom:sub_DB35.
comments.rom:DB35: The scatter->chase mode-switch handler, called from rom:sub_D69B's timer once the current phase's duration elapses. Sets ChaseModeFlag (ram_00FF) back to 0 (full chase-AI targeting, see rom:D777) and, for every ghost still in GhostState 0 (normal roaming, not eaten/housed), sets ram_214C,X -- a 'reverse direction' request flag also read by rom:sub_D6DE's movement code -- the classic arcade tell of a scatter/chase mode switch forcing every ghost to instantly reverse course. Then shifts ModeTimerNextLo/Hi (ram_216E/ram_216F) into ModeTimerTargetLo/Hi as the next phase's duration, resetting ram_216E/ram_216F to the $FF sentinel until something refills them. LIVE-VERIFIED: ChaseModeFlag genuinely toggles 0/1 throughout run-02.inp (first flips to 1 at frame 1435, matching wave start, then keeps alternating roughly every 500-3,000 frames) -- the mode-switch mechanism is real and active, though the actual duration schedule written into ram_216C-ram_216F was not found in the traced code. UPDATE, fully resolving the earlier 'schedule values not found' gap: LIVE-VERIFIED (tools/probe-modeschedule2.lua against run-02.inp) that the initial schedule seed is the LAST 4 bytes of whatever 32-byte dat_DF21 sub-block rom:sub_DE8B copies for the current MazeColorVariant -- i.e. the same per-wave maze-color-attribute copy dual-purposes its own tail as the mode-timer's initial (current, next) duration pair. For MazeColorVariant 0 this is exactly (ModeTimerTargetLo/Hi=$07/$A4, ModeTimerNextLo/Hi=$19/$54), confirmed landing in ram_216C-ram_216F at the observed wave-start frame. After the first two scheduled switches consume that seed pair (and ModeTimerNext resets to the $FF sentinel, as this routine's own code produces), live data shows ModeTimerNext getting REFILLED with real values anyway (alternating $01/$A4 and $06/$54, matching each switch exactly) for the rest of the recording -- meaning the schedule doesn't actually run dry after 2 switches as this routine's code alone would suggest. RESOLVED, correcting the 'not found' conclusion from a prior pass: rom:sub_DE8B is not game-start-only -- it also runs at every subsequent wave transition, reached via a second call path (rom:L_F6DA/rom:sub_CC73, off the maze-clear sequence around rom:F6C6) that a first pass missed. Each time it runs, it re-seeds the WHOLE mode-timer schedule fresh from the current wave's dat_DF21 sub-block -- not a partial 'refill' of just ram_216E/ram_216F at all. LIVE-CONFIRMED: WaveCounter visibly advances 0->1 at frame 6633 (tools/probe-schedulereseed.lua), immediately followed by ram_216C-ram_216F loading dat_DF21's wave-1 sub-block tail ($01,$A4,$06,$54) at frame 6651 -- exactly the value seen repeating afterward, because wave 1 and wave 2 happen to share an identical dat_DF21 tail, not because of any separate incremental refill mechanism.
comments.rom:DAC3: Power-pellet-eaten handler (called once from rom:L_D1FD). For every ghost not already eaten or mid-house-transit (GhostState 1 or 3), sets GhostFrightFlag (ram_2140,X) to $08 via rom:sub_D9EA -- the start of frightened/vulnerable mode -- and a nonzero speed-boost-cancel code in ram_2144,X. Frightened ghosts revert automatically the next time the per-wave movement-cadence counter completes a cycle (rom:sub_DAF8, called from rom:sub_DC44) rather than via any independent countdown -- an elegant reuse of the same per-wave period (dat_DCF9) that governs movement speed, which is also why fright duration gets shorter in later waves exactly the way movement gets faster: same underlying value, two effects.
comments.rom:E078: The actual ghost-eaten-while-frightened check, right after the shared fruit/ghost proximity test (dat_E0DD). Only scores if GhostFrightFlag (ram_2140,X) is exactly $08 -- confirming $08 specifically means 'currently vulnerable', not just 'nonzero'. On a hit: rom:sub_E097 handles the eaten-ghost housekeeping (score popup sprite, position reset) and rom:sub_DB20 sets GhostState (ram_2138,X) to 1 (eyes returning home) and GhostFrightFlag to $10 via rom:sub_D9DB. Earlier in this investigation $10 was guessed as a 'flashing, about to expire' warning sub-state -- RETRACTED, no evidence survived closer tracing; $10 is set here specifically as part of the per-ghost eaten cleanup, not a global fright-ending signal.
comments.rom:DB5B: CORRECTED from an earlier tentative read (this was carried into a prior session's notes as a 'fright-mode duration timer' -- wrong on closer tracing). GhostReleaseTimeout (ram_00F8) counts up against a WaveCounter-scaled threshold ($F0/240 frames for wave<5, $B4/180 for wave>=5 -- shorter in later waves), and once reached, checks GhostState (ram_2139/ram_213A/ram_213B -- i.e. ram_2138,X unrolled for slots 1/2/3 specifically, NOT slot 0) for whichever is still 4 (confined/waiting in house) and forces it to rom:sub_DAB6, transitioning that slot to state 2 (starts actually exiting). This is a time-based FORCED ghost-house release fallback -- distinct from the normal per-slot staggered release thresholds already found (dat_E8AA: 9/12/15/18) -- matching the arcade's classic dual dot-count/timeout release design, though whether this port also has a dot-count-linked release wasn't found this pass. UPDATE, resolving the 'does release also have a dot-count trigger' open item: no. DotsEatenCount (ram_00AA) is read in exactly two places in the whole ROM -- its own increment (rom:D240) and the Cruise Elroy speed check (rom:D78C) -- never anywhere near GhostReleaseTimeout, dat_E8AA, or the GhostState==4 release checks. This port's ghost-house release is driven purely by the two timer-based mechanisms already found (the per-slot staggered thresholds and this forced timeout); there's no dot-count-linked release the way the original arcade has.
comments.rom:D1E5: RESOLVED and LIVE-VERIFIED: the dot/power-pellet eating detector -- the last major open scoring question. Reads the tile code at Pac-Man's own position (rom:sub_F5FF, the same tile-buffer read/write pair the maze renderer uses, see dat_FBBC's note) and checks it: tile $51 -> a dot (rom:L_D20D, awards a raw BCD delta of 1 via rom:sub_F614 -- 10 points at the project's established x10 BCD scale). tile $52 or $53 (checked together via AND #$FE) -> a power pellet (rom:L_D1FD, calls rom:sub_DAC3 to start ghost-fright mode -- see 'Checking the ghost logic' -- then awards a raw BCD delta of 4, i.e. 40 points). Either way falls through into rom:sub_D21C, which immediately overwrites that tile with $50 (the blank/filler code seen throughout dat_FBBC/dat_FBDC) so it can't be eaten twice, increments DotsEatenCount (ram_00AA, newly named -- also read by the Cruise Elroy check), decrements DotsUntilFruit (ram_00AF, newly named -- reaching -1 triggers rom:sub_D508, the fruit-appearance routine), resets GhostReleaseTimeout back to 0 (eating a dot resets the ghost-house forced-release clock), and decrements a level-clear countdown (ram_00A8/ram_00A9 -> rom:sub_D26B once exhausted). LIVE-VERIFIED against run-02.inp (tools/probe-doteat.lua): Score climbed by exactly 1 raw BCD unit per dot for 40 consecutive dots while DotsEatenCount and DotsUntilFruit moved in perfect lockstep (DotsUntilFruit=56 minus DotsEatenCount, exactly, the whole way), then jumped by more than 1 at frame 2144 -- the exact same frame GhostFrightFlag was independently confirmed flipping to 8 for all four ghosts, i.e. this is the power-pellet-eaten event, not a coincidence.
comments.rom:DE8B: The maze wall-color/attribute loader, and (see dat_DF21's note) the scatter/chase mode-timer schedule seeder -- runs at every wave transition, not just game start (see rom:DB35's comment for the correction this enabled). Two independent lookups happen here, keyed by two different counters: (1) WaveCounter (clamped, via dat_DFE4) picks which 32-byte dat_DF21 sub-block to copy into ram_2150-ram_216F -- this is what actually determines the wall color AND the mode-timer seed. (2) MazeColorVariant (clamped at $12/18) separately indexes dat_DFD1 -> dat_DFC1/dat_DFC2 to set ram_00F9/ram_00FA -- the exact two thresholds rom:sub_D777's Blinky/Cruise-Elroy check compares against. So the 'Cruise Elroy' speed-boost thresholds are keyed by maze color variant, not wave number directly -- resolving the earlier open item about where those thresholds come from, though the actual speed effect (ram_2144 becoming nonzero) still isn't confirmed live against an actual movement-speed change.
comments.rom:F663: RESOLVED and LIVE-VERIFIED: the extra-life mechanism, the last item on this project's original open-questions list. ExtraLifeCountdown (ram_004A/ram_004B, newly named -- a 2-byte BCD counter sitting right after Score in RAM) is initialized from the tail of dat_D04C ($09,$99, i.e. BCD 0999) by rom:sub_CDD0 at game start -- the same routine that zeroes the actual score, since dat_D04C's first 4 bytes are the score's own zeroed initial value and the last 2 are this countdown's seed. Every score award (via rom:sub_F61A) also subtracts ScoreDeltaHi/Lo from this countdown in the same x10-scaled BCD units; once it goes negative, rom:sub_F6E8 fires (a bonus-life effect/jingle via rom:sub_EA36). At the x10 scale, BCD 0999 is 9,990 points -- close to but not exactly the classic arcade's round 10,000, and there's nothing wrong with that: this port's own threshold is simply 9,990. rom:sub_F67E is the identical mechanism for player 2 (ram_0050/ram_0051, seeded the same way). LIVE-VERIFIED against run-02.inp (tools/probe-extralife.lua): ExtraLifeCountdown starts at exactly 0999 and decrements by the exact point value of every score event seen (1 per dot, 4 at the power-pellet frame, matching amounts at each already-verified ghost-eaten frame) -- never reached long enough in this recording to see the actual trigger fire, but the countdown mechanism itself is fully confirmed. Not found: which specific RAM byte holds the on-screen 'lives remaining' count that presumably increments when rom:sub_F6E8 fires -- ram_00A3/ram_00A4, which it does touch, are also reused as general level-transition timing counters elsewhere, so they're likely just borrowed for jingle/pause timing rather than being the lives counter itself.
comments.rom:DEF7: RESOLVED: how the Cruise Elroy speed code (ram_2144,X, set by rom:sub_D777's Blinky check) actually becomes a speed difference. GhostState==1 (eaten) always returns 'yes, decide a move this tick'. Otherwise, ram_2144,X is used as a Y-index into the SAME ram_2150+ array rom:sub_DE8B copies wall-color/mode-timer data into (a third use for that one block of RAM) -- pulling out a single bit that gates whether this ghost's movement-decision logic runs at all this tick (via the AND #$01 + BEQ in rom:sub_D6CF, this routine's only caller). Different ram_2144 values select a different row of that data, sampling a different bit-pattern -- a duty-cycle throttle, not a distinct code path, so a 'faster' Elroy code is really just a row with more 1-bits, letting the movement decision through more often. RETRACTED, and instructive as to why: an earlier pass reported ram_2144 for slot 0 flipping 0->1 at frame 21685 in run-02.inp as 'Elroy activating live'. It wasn't. ram_2144,X is ALSO written unconditionally by rom:sub_DAC3 (fright start, value 1) and rom:sub_DAF8 (per-wave speed-cadence wrap, value 0) -- completely unrelated to Cruise Elroy, the same kind of RAM-slot reuse this project has hit before (see a7800-toolkit/docs/pitfalls.md). A follow-up probe cross-checking GhostFrightFlag at the same moment showed it flipping to 8 (frightened) on the EXACT SAME frame ram_2144 flipped to 1, and back at the exact frame GhostFrightFlag showed the eaten value (16) -- conclusively rom:sub_DAC3's fright-start write, not Elroy's #3/#4 codes at all. This also explains the 'value discrepancy' flagged in the original report: it wasn't a mis-traced threshold, it was two different writers of the same array slot. Genuine Cruise Elroy activation (value 3 or 4, gated on ram_213B==0 per rom:D777's comment) was never actually observed in this recording and remains unconfirmed live.
comments.rom:CCF9: RESOLVED and LIVE-VERIFIED, found while hunting for the lives-remaining counter (see rom:sub_CA95's comment for that search). This is the classic Ms. Pac-Man 'fruit tray' -- the row of fruit icons at the bottom-right showing every fruit type encountered so far this game, distinct from the bottom-left lives icons. FruitTrayCount (ram_0084, newly named) = min(WaveCounter, 7) + 1, i.e. 1-8. rom:sub_CEAB draws one fixed icon plus FruitTrayCount-1 more from dat_D05A (an 8-entry position table), each spaced 24 pixels apart. LIVE-VERIFIED against run-02.inp: a screenshot at frame 2200 (wave 0) shows an empty tray; a screenshot at frame 21,500 (wave 5) shows 5 fruit icons -- exactly matching the formula.
comments.rom:CDEE: The 2-player turn-swap. For X=$0B downto 0, swaps ram_00A4,X with ram_00E4,X -- 12 bytes each (ram_00A4-ram_00AF <-> ram_00E4-ram_00EF). Since WaveCounter (ram_00A6), MazeColorVariant (ram_00A5), MazeScheduleIndex (ram_00A7), DotsEatenCount (ram_00AA), and DotsUntilFruit (ram_00AF) all live inside this swapped 12-byte block, this confirms each player has fully independent progress through the game -- the 'currently active player' block always sits at ram_00A4-ram_00AF, and swapping stashes the other player's state at ram_00E4-ram_00EF between turns. Called at game start and at every wave transition (rom:sub_CC46/rom:CC49), i.e. every time control might hand off between players. Found while hunting for a lives-remaining counter -- none of the still-unnamed bytes in this swapped block (ram_00A8/A9/AB/AC/AD/AE) were confirmed as lives; see rom:sub_CA95's comment for that search's outcome.
comments.rom:CA95: The post-death/post-wave-clear dispatcher, reached once ram_00A2 is set (rom:L_F6E0, after the death or wave-clear countdown at ram_00A3/ram_00A4 finishes). Checks ram_009C (an HSC/High-Score-Cart-present flag, set at boot by rom:L_CBC2 via a signature check against $3900/$3904 -- NOT a lives counter, ruled out) to decide whether to detour through an HSC save/load step (rom:L_CAB0) before falling into the same title-screen/attract-mode-adjacent code (rom:sub_CAB6 onward) that handles the SWCHB game-select switch. NOT FOUND despite a real search: the lives-remaining counter itself. What was checked -- no `LDA #$05` (or `#$04`) exists anywhere in the ROM as a plausible '5 lives' constant; a full live baseline-and-diff scan of ram_0040-ram_00FF found one numeric candidate (ram_0067=5, matching the manual's 5-lives claim and the 4-icon tray visible on screen, see rom:sub_CEAB's neighbor for the confirmed fruit tray) but a direct fault-injection test -- live-patching ram_0067 to 1 mid-recording and screenshotting before/after -- produced no change in the on-screen icon row, ruling it out. The lives icons don't appear to be drawn via a DEX/DEY-loop call to rom:sub_EA36 (no such loop exists anywhere) or via the same tile-write routine (rom:sub_F5E9) the fruit tray uses in an obviously analogous way either -- genuinely unresolved, not just unchecked.

blocks.name: dat_C000
blocks.note: CONFIRMED no gaps-closing risk (checked across all 23 initial gap ranges as a batch): no JSR/JMP anywhere in the code traced so far lands inside this range. Byte-frequency signature -- 96 distinct values, dominated by $00/$55/$54/$15/$3F/$AA/$FF -- matches the dense, few-values-repeated bit-plane pattern the sibling 16K projects' actual graphics/character sheets all showed. Sits immediately before RESET ($CA20) at the very base of the mapped ROM window, with zero xrefs from any 6502 code traced so far -- consistent with Maria DMA-ing this directly as character/sprite data rather than the 6502 ever loading it by address, which is the normal, expected case for graphics data on this hardware (not a red flag the way a stray reachable-code gap would be). Declared as one block to close the gap; not decoded into individual tiles this pass. Cross-checked against this pass's other findings: the actual maze WALL-LAYOUT bitmaps turned out to live in the tail block (dat_FC7C, see rom:sub_FC18), and per-maze-variant COLOR/attribute data lives in dat_DF21 -- both a different kind of data than a raw graphics/character sheet. dat_C000's byte-frequency signature still doesn't match either of those; the original graphics/tile-sheet characterization stands, just now with two other candidate identities ruled out rather than merely un-checked.

blocks.name: dat_E342
blocks.note: RESOLVED, and it's not maze/level layout data -- the original guess (retracted once ram_2124 turned out not to behave like a small level index) was on the wrong track entirely. Read at rom:sub_E159 (LDX ram_2124 with no index -- i.e. actor slot 0's own position byte, which rom:sub_E0FB sets to a small 0/1/2 maze-variant index right before calling this), dat_E342 ($02,$04,$08 -- power-of-two bit flags) and its sibling dat_E345 ($03,$06,$09) select per-maze-variant type/flag parameters for the two actors sub_E159 spawns via sub_EA36. The many other small 3-entry tables declared across this whole span (dat_E348, dat_E34B, dat_E34E, and more) follow the same shape and almost certainly supply the rest of the per-variant position/type parameters for the already-solved intermission animation (see rom:E0FB/rom:E168 in docs/FINDINGS.md) -- this entire block is intermission-actor setup data, not a maze grid.

blocks.name: dat_EB75
blocks.note: RESOLVED, also not maze/level layout data. Read by sub_EB3A (rom:EB43/EB49, part of the actor-management family around sub_EA36/ActorActiveFlags), alongside its sibling dat_EB8A: given an actor-type code (Y), the pair produces a 16-bit ROM pointer (low byte from dat_EB75, high byte from dat_EB8A) stored into ram_1D0C/ram_1D10. dat_EB8A's values climb smoothly ($EB-$F2) the way pointer high bytes do for sequentially-laid-out data, while dat_EB75's look scattered the way low bytes always do -- a type-to-script/data-pointer table. The immediately neighboring sub_EB1E reads a similar indirect pointer (ram_00C8) into AUDV0 (the sound volume register), suggesting these per-type pointers lead to each actor type's own animation-and-sound script, not a level layout.

blocks.name: dat_F8C6
blocks.note: RESOLVED. Called from sub_F890 (rom:F890, the shared sprite/frame-lookup dispatcher hit from ~19 different call sites across ghosts/Pac-Man/fruit/score-digit drawing code). dat_F8C6 remaps an incoming character/sprite ID (Y) to an internal frame-group index, which is then compared against a fixed threshold ($13) to choose between two further per-frame graphics tables (dat_F952 / dat_FA1B). A character/sprite-ID indirection layer, not maze or level data.

blocks.name: dat_CF51
blocks.note: CONFIRMED no gaps-closing risk (see dat_C000's note -- same batch check, no stray JSR/JMP lands inside). Byte-frequency signature is mixed/scattered rather than matching either the graphics-tile or small-integer-tile pattern seen elsewhere -- consistent with jump tables, pointer tables, or other code-adjacent parameter data, the same family the Galaga project's own smaller gaps turned out to be. Declared as one block to close the gap; not characterized further this pass.

blocks.name: dat_DF21
blocks.note: RESOLVED. Read by sub_DE8B (rom:DE8B, called from rom:CC7C during setup): 32-byte chunks of dat_DF21 are copied into ram_2150+ (the maze's rendered color/attribute RAM), with the source offset chosen by WaveCounter alone (via a dat_DFE4 remap) -- CORRECTED: an earlier pass in this same note wrongly said MazeColorVariant also picks the source offset; closer reading of rom:sub_DE8B's tail shows MazeColorVariant is used AFTER this copy for a completely separate purpose (see rom:DE8B's own comment: the Cruise Elroy speed-threshold lookup), not to select which dat_DF21 sub-block gets copied. This is per-maze-color-variant wall attribute/palette data -- likely the actual ROM form of the manual's 'four different maze patterns', confirming MazeColorVariant's role as their selector. UPDATE: the last 4 bytes of each 32-byte per-variant sub-block turn out to be dual-purpose -- confirmed LIVE (see rom:DB35's comment) as the initial scatter/chase mode-timer schedule seed (ModeTimerTargetLo/Hi, ModeTimerNextLo/Hi), copied into ram_216C-ram_216F by the exact same sub_DE8B copy that installs the wall-color/attribute data. One data block, two uses.

blocks.name: dat_DCCD
blocks.note: RESOLVED. Read by sub_DA32 (rom:DA32, called from rom:CC79, part of new-game/new-life actor reset): dat_DCCD (4 bytes) and its immediate sibling dat_DCD1 (4 bytes, also declared inside this span) are copied into ram_2120,X and ram_2124,X for X=0-3 -- a per-actor (4 slots: Pac-Man plus 3 ghosts, or the 4 ghosts) INITIAL POSITION table. This also resolves the earlier retracted guess about ram_2124: it's each actor's own live position coordinate (this table supplies its small reset value at spawn time; the much larger values seen live mid-game, e.g. 47/38/111, are just the actor having moved since then -- not evidence against a position byte, as the original retraction worried).

blocks.name: dat_D614
blocks.note: RESOLVED. Read by a position-refinement routine at rom:D49E (rom:D4BC), indexed by a 4-entry rotating counter (ram_2117): dat_D614 is $FF,$FF,$01,$01 -- a small four-step (-1,-1,+1,+1) delta cycle added into the live coordinate, consistent with a sub-pixel/fine movement-smoothing step rather than a lookup table in the level-data sense.

blocks.name: dat_F52C
blocks.note: RESOLVED. Read directly inside ENTRY_Nmi's live display-list-entry construction (rom:F388/F38E, executed every vblank), alongside its sibling dat_F54B (also declared inside this span): together they supply the low/high bytes of a per-row Maria graphics-data pointer, written into the working display list at ram_1F00/ram_1F02 for the row-group indexed by ram_0055. dat_F52C's values step by roughly $1C (28) per entry, matching the same 28-byte row stride found in the maze-wall renderer -- graphics/display-list plumbing, not gameplay data.

blocks.name: dat_D3E1
blocks.note: RESOLVED. Read by sub_D2B4 (rom:D2B4, called from 7 sites across actor start/reset code), indexed by X = (ram_2105<<2)|ram_2104 -- a composite of two small per-actor state fields (direction and phase, most likely). dat_D3E1 and its sibling dat_D3ED (also declared inside this span) feed ram_0068/ram_006E, both used elsewhere as position-seed scratch -- a per-direction/phase starting-offset table for (re)spawning an actor.

blocks.name: dat_FBBC
blocks.note: RESOLVED, and directly tied to the actual maze-wall renderer. Read from rom:sub_FC00/L_FB07 alongside its sibling dat_FBDC (also declared inside this span): given a packed bit index X (built from a maze bitmap byte, see rom:sub_FC18/ram_1C00 below), dat_FBBC/dat_FBDC each supply one of two WALL-SEGMENT TILE CODES that get poked into the screen's tile buffer via an indirect pointer that advances by $1C (28, the maze's row width) per row. The two tables hold the SAME set of tile-code values ($30-$3C) in genuinely different orders, not a mirror of each other -- consistent with Ms. Pac-Man's mazes not being simple left-right mirrors (unlike the original Pac-Man's), each needing its own wall-corner/edge tile assignment per bit position. This is the maze-layout data the user expected to find, just encoded as a compact wall bitmap (see rom:FC18) decoded through this autotile-style lookup, not a literal per-cell grid.

blocks.name: dat_E970
blocks.note: Read by sub_E91F (rom:E921, an init routine) to fill a 32-byte RAM buffer (ram_1800) while a parallel buffer (ram_1A00) gets a fixed $1D in every slot. Contains embedded ROM-address-shaped byte pairs ($E9,$7F / $E9,$00,$1A / $E9,$6F -- i.e. $E97F/$E96F, both inside this same data region) mixed with small integers -- plausibly a HUD/attract-text row template with some embedded pointers, but not decoded far enough to say what it renders as. UPDATE: stronger characterization found by tracing further. ram_1800/ram_1A00 (this block's copy destinations) aren't a dedicated array at all -- rom:sub_CC8B zero-clears a full 1KB scratch region (ram_1800-ram_1BFF, four pages) at boot, reused by multiple unrelated systems afterward; this is just one transient use. The neighboring routine (rom:sub_E94A, reading dat_FA1B,Y) confirmed the family: nonzero source bytes get SEC/SBC #$5E (a fixed subtraction, converting an encoded byte into a small tile-code), while a zero source byte is treated as a delimiter and substituted with the same $1D 'blank' filler seen in dat_E970's own copy -- the shape of an encoded-text-to-tile-code string renderer (likely a game-over/message system, given the neighboring code also touches FruitTypeFloor and branches on player number). Confirmed as part of a text-rendering subsystem; the exact message content wasn't decoded this pass.

blocks.name: dat_E0DD
blocks.note: RESOLVED. Read from two near-identical routines (rom:E01C, fruit-eating distance check; rom:E039, ghost-collision distance check) as a per-axis hitbox threshold: given the distance already computed on one axis (Y), dat_E0DD gives the max allowed distance on the other axis for a 'close enough' hit. Its six values (5,4,3,2,1,0) form a diamond-shaped falloff -- a compact approximation of a circular collision radius, shared by both the fruit and the ghost collision checks.

blocks.name: dat_DE73
blocks.note: RESOLVED, by tracing the full surrounding routine rather than just the immediate read site. This is the ghost intersection turn-decision cost table -- the actual mechanism behind rom:sub_D713's 'pick a direction toward the target' logic. rom:sub_DE2E first computes a preferred axis: X-distance vs Y-distance to the target (already computed by rom:sub_DDF5), producing a direction code 0-7 in ScoreDeltaHi (reused as scratch here, unrelated to score) that says 'prefer horizontal, this sign' or 'prefer vertical, this sign'. rom:L_DE15 then, for each of the (up to 4) candidate exit directions at a junction (X), adds that preferred-direction code to X and indexes dat_DE73 -- a 4x4 matrix with -1 on the diagonal and a single +1 off-diagonal band per row -- to get a small cost adjustment added to the summed distance. Directions matching the preferred axis/sign score lowest (the diagonal's -1), giving the classic Pac-Man ghost pathfinding rule (always lean toward the target on whichever axis has the bigger remaining gap) a concrete tie-breaking shape rather than a hard binary choice.

blocks.name: dat_F5A6
blocks.note: RESOLVED. Read by sub_F594 (rom:F5A2) right after reading SWCHA and masking to a 4-bit up/down/left/right switch nibble -- this is the joystick raw-switch-pattern to direction-code decode table (16 entries, one per possible SWCHA nibble), the standard input-decoding table every sibling project has had one of.

blocks.name: dat_E9BD
blocks.note: UNRESOLVED, flagged rather than characterized. Zero static xrefs found anywhere in the traced 52% of code, yet the 17 bytes decode cleanly as a real, self-contained generic page/block-copy routine: LDY #$00 / LDA ($B2),Y / STA ($B0),Y / DEY / BNE (inner loop) / INC $B1 / INC $B3 / DEX / BNE (outer loop) / RTS -- copies 256*X bytes from a source pointer at $B2/$B3 to a dest pointer at $B0/$B1. No indirect-jump instruction exists anywhere in the code traced so far that could reach this address dynamically, so, like dat_F83C nearby, this is either genuinely unreached/dead code or a coincidental decode of real data. Left as a declared block rather than asserted as code. UPDATE: checked more rigorously on request -- a raw byte scan of the entire ROM (not just the disassembled listing) for JSR/JMP with this address as a literal operand (zero hits), every JMP-indirect ($6C) opcode anywhere in the ROM as a possible RAM-vector call (14 hits, all confirmed coincidental data/operand bytes by hand), and the classic RTS-trick push-then-RTS idiom for this address (no hits). Still unresolved -- this rules out the common indirect-call shapes, not every possible mechanism. RESOLVED, by a technique this project hadn't used before: read taps (mem:install_read_tap) on the block's exact byte range, run against all 4 recordings, to check empirically whether anything ever touches these bytes at all -- rather than only searching statically for a caller. Something DOES read every byte of this block, identically across all 4 recordings regardless of length, early in each run (frame ~14-160). The read-tap's own cpu.state PC report was a constant, bogus-looking value ($2404, a RAM address) for every hit -- not a MAME bug: stack-peeking at the moment of each read (reading the return address pushed by whatever JSR led here) traced it to a real, genuine piece of 6502 code sitting in RAM at $23FF, itself invoked from a small dispatcher also in RAM ($238F/$23B7/...). That RAM code is self-modifying -- one operand byte (which 256-byte ROM PAGE to sweep) gets patched before each call, seen live patched to $E9, $F8, and $D4 across different invocations, sweeping this block's own page along with everything else on it, byte by byte, into an accumulator and a lookup table -- the shape of a checksum/verification pass, not meaningful execution of this block's own bytes as instructions. The RAM template's own bytes were traced back further: they match a prefix found at a fixed offset (1279) in the actual Atari 7800 system BIOS ROM file (7800ntsc.u7 / '7800 BIOS (U).rom'), confirmed by direct byte comparison -- this is BIOS-level cartridge-checksum code, copied into RAM and run at boot, completely external to Ms. Pac-Man's own cartridge code. So: yes, every run does read these bytes, but never as part of the GAME's own logic -- the original 'no caller found anywhere in this ROM' conclusion was correct for what it claimed (no in-cartridge caller exists) and remains true; it just wasn't the full answer to whether the bytes are ever touched at all. Not pursued further: exactly what the BIOS's checksum protects or verifies, since that's BIOS behavior, out of scope for this cartridge disassembly. In relation to the game, if it ever ran: a general N*256-byte page copy from a source pointer at $B2/$B3 to a dest pointer at $B0/$B1 -- the same scratch-pointer convention the tile-buffer and graphics-pointer routines use elsewhere. Bigger and more general than anything the shipped game's actual bulk copies need (the maze bitmap load is 128 bytes, the display-list graphics copy ~88 bytes, both hand-unrolled fixed loops) -- reads like a general-purpose copy utility superseded once the real data sizes were known.

blocks.name: dat_E9F7
blocks.note: RESOLVED. Read by sub_E999 (rom:E99A, called from the same position-update family as rom:sub_D49E), added directly onto a live coordinate: $01,$00,$FF,$00 -- the standard 4-direction (+1,0,-1,0) unit movement-delta table for one axis. A same-shaped sibling almost certainly backs the other axis via sub_E99E.

blocks.name: dat_E8AA
blocks.note: RESOLVED. Read at rom:E74C inside a wait-loop gating an actor's release (alongside a companion check at rom:sub_E731 comparing ram_2124,X against a fixed $23) -- the values 9,12,15,18 (each +3) are per-ghost-slot thresholds, giving each of the 4 ghost slots its own staggered release delay. Likely the actual ghost-house exit timing the manual doesn't detail.

blocks.name: dat_DC6B
blocks.note: RESOLVED, from the earlier speed-mechanism investigation (see docs/FINDINGS.md, 'Why the Teddy Bear start runs slowly'). dat_DC6B and its sibling dat_DC70 (also declared inside this span) are the five-entry movement-cadence checkpoint tables read by rom:sub_DC44: a per-wave period counter (SpeedCountdown/ram_00DC) only produces an actual movement step on the frames where its value matches one of these checkpoints, which is what turns a bigger starting period (from dat_DCF9, indexed by WaveCounter) into visibly slower motion.

blocks.name: dat_FC7C
blocks.note: CONFIRMED no gaps-closing risk (see dat_C000's note). Runs to the ROM's own top and includes the hardware vectors at $FFFA-$FFFF (NMI=$F34D, RESET=$CA20, IRQ=$F41C -- byte-verified against the already-declared entries), the same reason this showed as a gap in every sibling project (vector bytes are data, not executed code).
